title: Nexus
description: Full-stack project management application with authentication, task tracking, Kanban board, and analytics. Built with Next.js App Router, Server Actions, and Prisma.

caseStudy.projectOverview: Nexus is a full-stack project management application built with Next.js 15 App Router. It covers authentication, project and task management, Kanban workflows, and an analytics dashboard. It started as a client-only frontend consuming an external REST API and has since moved to a server-first architecture using Server Components, Server Actions, and Prisma ORM, making it a migration exercise as much as a product. Nexus is intentionally an ongoing project developed in cycles: I pause it to explore other products, then return with new ideas, architectural improvements, and lessons learned elsewhere. Rather than targeting a fixed final state, it acts as a long-term environment for evolving my full-stack, product, and SaaS practices.
whyThisStack: Next.js App Router enables Server Components and Server Actions, which removed the need for a separate API layer and a client-side state management library
Prisma ORM provides type-safe database access that integrates cleanly with TypeScript and keeps schema and queries in sync
Auth.js v5 handles the full authentication lifecycle (sessions, OAuth, and credentials) with Edge-compatible middleware for route protection
A centralised ActionResult type with Zod validation keeps Server Actions consistent, with errors surfaced to the UI in a uniform pattern
keyFeatures: Google OAuth and email/password authentication with password reset flow and rate limiting
Database queries scoped by user to keep each account's data isolated
Task management with filtering, pagination, tagging, and status tracking
Analytics dashboard with priority distribution and tasks-by-status charts
Reusable Server Actions with a centralised ActionResult type and Zod validation
challengesTradeoffs: Migrating incrementally from React Query and Axios to Server Actions without breaking existing features
Designing a scalable actions architecture, splitting monolithic files into co-located per-action modules with tests
Balancing server-side simplicity with client interactivity by using the 'use client' boundary carefully
Maintaining architectural consistency in a long-running project that evolves through separate development cycles
nextSteps: Explore SaaS foundations: multi-user workspaces and billing

title: Redirect Lab
description: Full-stack link management platform with custom short URLs, access tracking, cross-tab synchronisation, accessible interactions, infinite scrolling, and CSV export through Cloudflare R2.

caseStudy.projectOverview: Redirect Lab is a full-stack link management platform built with an independent React client and Fastify API. It evolved from an earlier project and was rebuilt with a new identity, independently deployable repositories, stronger accessibility and testing practices, and a cost-conscious cloud architecture. The goal was to turn a basic URL shortener into a maintainable portfolio product with a focused user experience, reliable state handling, automated quality checks, and infrastructure that can run at little or no cost.
whyThisStack: React and TanStack Query provide a focused client architecture with explicit server-state caching, mutation feedback, and paginated data loading
Fastify and Drizzle ORM create a lightweight, type-safe API and persistence layer that stays aligned with the TypeScript domain model
Vitest, Testing Library, and axe-core support fast behavioral and accessibility testing without adding external testing services
Vercel, Railway, Neon, and Cloudflare R2 provide independently deployable infrastructure with practical free or low-cost tiers
keyFeatures: Custom short URL creation with validation and duplicate prevention
Cross-tab access count synchronisation through BroadcastChannel, without additional real-time infrastructure
Paginated link loading with infinite scrolling and IntersectionObserver
CSV export stored on Cloudflare R2 and delivered through a public URL
Accessible forms, dialogs, controls, and focus states, with automated axe checks
challengesTradeoffs: Separating the original monorepo while preserving history and letting the client and API evolve independently
Replacing the original AWS delivery setup with lower-cost services without losing deployment reliability
Keeping access counts synchronised across tabs without adding WebSockets or an external real-time service
Protecting delivery scope by postponing authentication and advanced analytics until the core product was stable
nextSteps: Build an access analytics dashboard with clicks grouped by period
Add QR Code generation and PNG download

title: Auth Starter
description: Reusable Next.js authentication foundation created to remove repetitive setup from new projects. Split into a clean template and a public documentation and demo site.

caseStudy.projectOverview: Auth Starter is a reusable authentication foundation for Next.js applications. It was created after noticing that authentication, database configuration, protected routes, social login, and password recovery required similar setup across many small projects. The project separates the reusable template from its public website, documentation, and future live demo.
caseStudy.problemPurpose: Repeatedly rebuilding authentication infrastructure was slowing down the start of new product experiments. The goal is to provide a secure, understandable, and reusable foundation that lets new projects begin closer to the product logic.
myFocus: Designing a reusable architecture without product-specific assumptions
Keeping the template separate from marketing and documentation code
Choosing current stable technologies and sensible security defaults
Creating a setup that remains understandable for developers without deep backend experience
whyThisStack: Next.js App Router provides server-rendered routes, Route Handlers, and a clear boundary between public and protected application areas
Better Auth offers a stable modern API for credentials, OAuth, sessions, and password recovery
Prisma and PostgreSQL provide type-safe relational persistence that can be reused across different products
Resend provides a focused transactional email integration for password recovery
Separating the site and template repositories prevents generated projects from inheriting portfolio and documentation code
keyFeatures: Reusable email and password authentication flow
Password recovery flow with transactional email support
Separate public site and clean template repositories
Adaptive visual identity and favicon for light and dark browser themes
challengesTradeoffs: Defining what belongs to the reusable template and what belongs only to the public demonstration site
Choosing Better Auth stable instead of building the starter on the still-beta Auth.js v5 API
Balancing a complete authentication foundation with a template that remains small and easy to understand
Planning for future automation without prematurely introducing the complexity of a CLI
whatILearned: Reusable foundations require stricter separation of responsibilities than product-specific applications
Documentation should follow a validated implementation instead of defining behavior too early
A template repository and an installable package solve different problems
Version stability is an important architectural consideration for reusable developer tooling
nextSteps: Finish and validate the template against a clean PostgreSQL database
Test credentials, Google OAuth, password recovery, and protected routes end to end
Publish the documentation and live demo site
Evaluate a future create-nextjs-auth-starter CLI after using the template in real projects
